articles.headline: FMI/FMU: Open Model‑Exchange Standard for Co‑Simulation alongside Simulink
articles.summary: The Functional Mock‑up Interface (FMI) defines an open format (FMU) for packaging dynamic models so they can be exchanged and co‑simulated across tools. It works with model‑based design environments such as Simulink, but does not provide its own modeling, calibration, or code‑generation capabilities. FMUs can be imported into other simulators, test rigs, or custom Python/C++ frameworks, enabling cross‑tool verification without abandoning the existing Simulink workflow.
articles.why_it_matters: For a Vehicle Control Unit developer, FMI lets you validate control algorithms against vehicle‑level models built in different environments (e.g., a powertrain model in Modelica). This reduces vendor lock‑in and eases integration testing of EV powertrain functions before hardware deployment.
articles.current_stack: Tool-specific Simulink model exchange and co-simulation
articles.relationship: Open standard that complements proprietary modeling tools
articles.comparison_note: FMI complements the current Simulink‑only model exchange by providing a tool‑agnostic container; it does not replace Simulink for model creation, calibration in INCA, or CAN analysis in CANalyzer. The standard covers model interface definition and execution packaging, but the underlying model authoring and code generation remain proprietary.
articles.limitations: FMI standardizes model interfaces and execution packaging; it does not replace the modeling, calibration, or code-generation tool used to create a model.
articles.practical_example: Export a simple torque‑control Simulink model as an FMU (Model → Export → FMU). Then, in Python using the PyFMI library, load the FMU, drive the input torque command, and plot the resulting speed response. Compare the result with a native Simulink simulation to verify identical behavior.
key_concepts: Limitations: no modeling or calibration functionality
interview_questions: How would you use FMI to integrate a powertrain model developed in Modelica with a VCU control algorithm built in Simulink?
What are the differences between FMI Model Exchange and Co‑Simulation, and when would you choose one over the other in an EV control validation workflow?
articles.next_step: Follow the official FMI tutorial to export a Simulink model as an FMU and run it in an open‑source simulator such as Dymola, OpenModelica, or PyFMI.

articles.headline: Key Testing & Validation Trends from Automotive Testing Expo NA 2026
articles.summary: The conference report outlines emerging approaches to automotive testing, emphasizing model‑in‑the‑loop (MiL), hardware‑in‑the‑loop (HiL), and automated test‑data management for powertrain control units. It highlights updates to ISO 26262, ISO 21434, and the growing role of open‑source test frameworks and cloud‑based validation pipelines. Sessions also covered real‑time CAN/LIN simulation tools and strategies for EV‑specific thermal and battery management testing.
articles.why_it_matters: VCU developers must align their MATLAB/Simulink models with the latest HiL and automated test workflows to meet safety and cybersecurity standards. Understanding these trends helps engineers integrate open‑source validation tools alongside CANalyzer/INCA, reducing test cycle time for EV powertrain software.
key_concepts: Model‑in‑the‑loop (MiL) and hardware‑in‑the‑loop (HiL) integration for VCU verification
ISO 26262 functional safety and ISO 21434 cybersecurity testing updates
Open‑source test automation frameworks (e.g., Open‑Test, ROS‑based test benches)
Cloud‑enabled test data management and analytics
Real‑time CAN/LIN simulation for EV battery‑management validation
interview_questions: How would you design a HiL test setup to validate the torque control algorithm of an EV VCU while ensuring ISO 26262 compliance?
Describe how you could incorporate an open‑source test automation framework with existing CANalyzer scripts to improve regression testing efficiency.
articles.next_step: Set up a small HiL loop using an open‑source CAN simulator (e.g., cantools) linked to a Simulink VCU model and execute a basic torque‑request test case, documenting the safety and data‑logging workflow.
